# `async`/`await` and IO

A program waiting on a file or the network spends most of its time doing nothing. The
`async`/`await` model lets it work on something else while it waits, without spawning threads. Nim
provides `std/asyncdispatch`. This chapter uses `Future`, `await`, and `waitFor` for sequences whose
output is always the same.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can mark a procedure with `{.async.}`, call it with `await`, run several
tasks at once with `all`, and read the error "Can only 'await' inside a proc marked as 'async'" when
`await` lands in the wrong place.
:::

## Async procedures and `Future`

An async procedure does not return a value directly. It returns a `Future`, a container that will
hold the result later. Save the following as `main.nim`, then run `nim c -r main.nim`.

```{.nim}
import std/asyncdispatch

proc greeting(name: string): Future[string] {.async.} =
  return "hello, " & name

proc main() {.async.} =
  let message = await greeting("Nim")
  echo message

waitFor main()
```

```{.txt}
hello, Nim
```

Notice three things. The `{.async.}` pragma rewrites the procedure so that `return` inside it fills a
`Future`. Inside `main`, `await greeting("Nim")` waits until the result is ready, then unwraps it.
Outside an async procedure, `waitFor` drives the async machinery until the task finishes.

`waitFor` starts the event loop, the mechanism that cycles through tasks that are waiting. That is
why it is called once, at the top level of the program.

`Future` is a generic type. `Future[string]` holds a string, `Future[int]` holds an integer.
`waitFor` returns the same value as the contents of that `Future`, so `let total = waitFor sum()`
gives you a plain `int`, not another container.

Why not just use threads? Threads are expensive and share memory, so they need locking and invite
races. The async model uses one thread and cycles through tasks that are waiting. A thousand
connections waiting for a reply do not mean a thousand threads; there are just a thousand small
`Future` values.

## Waiting in sequence

Each `await` waits for that task to finish before the next line runs.

```{.nim}
import std/asyncdispatch

proc fetch(name: string, delayMs: int): Future[string] {.async.} =
  await sleepAsync(delayMs)
  return name & " ready"

proc main() {.async.} =
  let first = await fetch("alpha", 30)
  echo first
  let second = await fetch("beta", 10)
  echo second

waitFor main()
```

```{.txt}
alpha ready
beta ready
```

Both tasks finish in order: `alpha` first, then `beta`, even though `beta` has the shorter delay.
This is what to watch when the program feels slow. Two `await` calls in a row add their delays, they
do not overlap them.

When the order really must be sequential, there is nothing wrong with this pattern. What is wrong is
reaching for it when the two tasks do not actually depend on each other.

## Stacking tasks with `all`

To run several tasks together, start them all first, then wait for them together.

```{.nim}
import std/asyncdispatch

proc fetch(name: string, delayMs: int): Future[string] {.async.} =
  await sleepAsync(delayMs)
  return name & " ready"

proc main() {.async.} =
  let results = await all(fetch("alpha", 30), fetch("beta", 10))
  for result in results:
    echo result

waitFor main()
```

```{.txt}
alpha ready
beta ready
```

`all` takes several `Future` values and returns one `Future` holding a sequence of results. The
order of the results follows the order of the arguments, not the order in which they finished. So
the output is still `alpha` then `beta`, even though `beta` finished first.

The difference shows up in time. Two tasks with 30 and 10 millisecond delays finish in about 30
milliseconds, not 40. For two tasks the gap is small; for two hundred network requests it is large.

As long as the tasks do not depend on each other, grouping them is almost always faster than waiting
for them one at a time.

One easy mistake: plain `sleep` blocks the entire event loop, whereas `sleepAsync` hands control back
to the async machinery. Inside an `{.async.}` procedure, use the async version of every waiting
operation. Otherwise the tasks run in sequence again without you noticing.

An error inside an async procedure surfaces when its `Future` is awaited. That means `try` and
`except` go around the `await`, not inside the procedure that raises. When several tasks are combined
with `all`, one failing task fails the whole combination.

## Deliberate error: `await` outside an async procedure

`await` is legal only inside a procedure marked `{.async.}`.

```{.nim}
import std/asyncdispatch

proc work(): Future[int] {.async.} =
  return 42

proc main(): int =
  let value = await work()
  value

echo main()
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(7, 25) Error: Can only 'await' inside a proc marked as 'async'. Use 'waitFor' when calling an 'async' proc in a non-async scope instead
```

The message has two parts. The first states the rule. The second hands you the way out: use
`waitFor` when the caller is not an async procedure. `(7, 25)` points at the line and column where
`await` sits.

There are two reasonable fixes. Turn `main` into an async procedure and call it with `waitFor`, or
leave `main` synchronous and call `waitFor work()` inside it.

There is also `asyncCheck` for starting a task without waiting for it. Be careful with it: if that
task fails and nothing waits for the result, the error is seen by nobody. Use `await` while the
result or the error actually matters.

## Exercises

1. Change the sequential example so the two tasks run together. Explain the difference in time.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/asyncdispatch

   proc tag(name: string): Future[string] {.async.} =
     return "tag:" & name

   proc main() {.async.} =
     echo await tag("a")
     echo await tag("b")

   waitFor main()
   ```
3. Write an async procedure that takes two `Future[int]` values, adds their results, then call it
   with `waitFor`.
4. Fix code that uses `await` inside an ordinary procedure, without changing what it is meant to do.

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- An `{.async.}` procedure returns a `Future`; `await` unwraps its result.
- `waitFor` drives the async machinery from synchronous code and is called once at the top level.
- Sequential `await` adds delays; `all` overlaps them and keeps argument order.
- The examples keep their output fixed by relying on `await` order, not on time.
- `await` outside an async procedure is rejected at compile time.
